best_for: Developers who want a free editor that handles most languages through extensions and want Microsoft's own add-ons such as Remote Development and the C# tools.
description:
Visual Studio Code is a code editor from Microsoft. It knows JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML and CSS out of the box, and language extensions add code completion, linting and debugging for Python, Java, C++ and many more. Its roadmap, plans and issue list are public on GitHub.

You can write, test and debug code in one window, set your own keyboard shortcuts, and arrange the layout to suit you. The same editor also runs in a web browser at vscode.dev. You can work inside a container, on another machine over SSH, or in WSL on Windows. Microsoft also lets you hand tasks to AI agents inside the editor, run by Copilot, Claude or Codex, and review their changes before you keep them.

points.title: Free for work too
points.text: Microsoft says VS Code is free for private and commercial use. The download is Microsoft's build of the MIT-licensed Code - OSS project, released under a Microsoft product license with some proprietary parts such as the Marketplace link.

points.title: Telemetry is on by default
points.text: VS Code sends usage data and crash reports to Microsoft. Set Telemetry Level to `off` in Settings to stop it, though extensions can still collect their own data.

points.title: Copilot is optional
points.text: You do not need Copilot to use the editor. Signing in with a GitHub account enrolls you in Copilot Free, which comes with a monthly allowance of inline suggestions and AI credits; paid Copilot plans or your own model keys go further.

points.title: Pick user or system setup on Windows
points.text: The user installer needs no admin rights and updates quietly in the background. The system installer goes into Program Files for all users, and updates need elevation. Both come for x64 and ARM64.

points.title: Linux: the Flatpak is not Microsoft's
points.text: Microsoft's Linux guide lists official .deb, .rpm and Snap packages. The Flatpak listed here names Microsoft as developer but is not verified on Flathub, and Microsoft's guide does not mention it.

points.title: Supported systems
points.text: 64-bit Windows client versions are supported, Windows Server is not. On macOS, Microsoft supports releases that still get Apple security updates. Linux needs glibc 2.28 or later, such as Ubuntu 20.04, Debian 10, RHEL 8 or Fedora 36.

points.title: Downgrades live on Windows
points.text: The Windows listing keeps 201 versions. macOS and Linux list only the current release, so going back there needs another source.
